ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Obstetrics and Gynecology Consultation — Marilyn Monroe — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Transvaginal ultrasound result and gynecology consultation: diagnosis, surgery, and fertility counseling

text.paragraph: Suspected endometriosis in a 30-year-old actor with severe painful periods since her teens, pelvic pain between periods, deep pain with intercourse, and painful bowel movements during periods, who wants children in a year or two. She started naproxen and a continuous combined pill on the day of this referral. Please confirm the diagnosis, advise on hormonal treatment and on whether and when surgery would help, and counsel her about fertility. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within two weeks, on the day of her transvaginal ultrasound. [S]

list.item: Does she have endometriosis, and is a transvaginal ultrasound enough to diagnose it, or is a laparoscopy needed?
Is the continuous combined pill the right first treatment, given that she wants a pregnancy in about a year, and what should follow if it fails?
Would surgery help her now, and how should the risks of ovarian surgery to her fertility be weighed?
How should her fertility be assessed and her pregnancy planned?
What non-drug treatments would help her pain, and do you agree with avoiding opioids and sedatives?

text.paragraph: Ms. Monroe, a 30-year-old actor, is seen at the request of Dr. Whitlock on the day of her transvaginal ultrasound. Her periods have been painful since her teens and have become disabling over three years, with pain between periods, deep pain with intercourse, and painful bowel movements during periods. She has never been pregnant. She started a continuous combined pill and naproxen nine days ago and has had no bleeding since; the pelvic ache is a little less. She does not smoke and has no migraine with aura. She wants children and is frightened that endometriosis or an operation will prevent it; she would like to try for a pregnancy in about a year. She is working with the clinic's behavioral health clinician on low mood and sleep. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: She was born Norma Jeane Mortenson on June 1, 1926, at Los Angeles General Hospital. Her father's identity is unconfirmed; her mother was often confined to asylums, and she spent her childhood in orphanages and foster homes. [D]

She worked as a photographic model, signed with Twentieth Century-Fox in 1946 under the name Marilyn Monroe, starred in films of the 1950s including Gentlemen Prefer Blondes and The Seven Year Itch, and studied at the Actors Studio in the mid-1950s. [D]
Her mother, Gladys, was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and was institutionalized, for the first time at the state hospital in Norwalk. [D]

She is described as one of the most famous people with endometriosis. Her biographer Anthony Summers wrote that the condition was so severe that it destroyed her marriages, her wish for children, her career and ultimately her life; a review of endometriosis for clinicians quotes this account, and museum and medical-history writers list endometriosis among her health problems. [D]

The same biographical account holds that, in the days before effective conservative surgery or medical therapy, her endometriosis led to progressively increasing use of strong analgesics, tranquilizers and hypnotics, and to drug dependency. [R]

The physician and historian Howard Markel writes that she had several mental health problems, including substance abuse, depression and, most likely, bipolar disorder, as well as endometriosis and gall bladder disease. [R]
Most of the drugs she misused had been prescribed to her by physicians; they included the barbiturate Nembutal and chloral hydrate. [D]

A retrospective psychological autopsy based on biographies, films and her writings proposes autism spectrum traits progressing to borderline personality disorder and bipolar disorder; the roster lists borderline personality disorder and depression. [R]

list.item: Endometriosis with a left ovarian endometrioma (N80.102). Her symptoms, the examination and a typical endometrioma on ultrasound establish endometriosis. The ESHRE guideline no longer requires laparoscopy for diagnosis when imaging shows an endometrioma or deep disease, so no surgery is needed to confirm it. There is no deep disease of the bowel or bladder. A continuous combined pill with an anti-inflammatory is the right first-line treatment and also covers contraception for the coming year; progestin alone or a GnRH antagonist with add-back would be the next steps if it fails. Surgery does not improve her chances of pregnancy at this stage and removing an endometrioma lowers the ovarian reserve, and each repeat operation lowers it further; surgery is kept for pain that does not respond, a growing cyst, or atypical imaging, and should then be a single, complete excision by an experienced surgeon. Her ovarian reserve is typical for her age. Most women with endometriosis conceive; hormonal treatment does not improve fertility and should be stopped when she wants to conceive. I agree with avoiding opioids and sedatives: pain from endometriosis is long-lasting, and these medicines add risk without treating the cause. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Whitlock's intake note. Transvaginal ultrasound today: a 3.4 by 2.9 cm unilocular cyst in the left ovary with uniform ground-glass contents, no solid parts and no internal blood flow, typical of an endometrioma; left ovary against the back of the uterus; the bowel slides freely behind the uterus; no deep nodule of the bowel, rectovaginal septum or bladder; uterus normal in size without signs of adenomyosis; right ovary normal; antral follicles 9 right and 6 left. Anti-Mullerian hormone 2.6 ng/mL. Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL. Urine pregnancy test negative at intake; gonorrhea, chlamydia and urinalysis negative. PHQ-9 12 and GAD-7 8 at intake. [S]

list.item: Continue ethinyl estradiol 0.02 mg with norethindrone acetate 1 mg daily without a pill-free week, and naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food on pain days, no more than 10 days a month. [S]
No laparoscopy now; repeat transvaginal ultrasound in about four months, then yearly or if symptoms change. [S]
If pain is not controlled after three to six months, change to norethindrone acetate alone or a GnRH antagonist with add-back therapy before considering surgery. [S]

Keep surgery in reserve for pain that does not respond, a growing cyst, or atypical imaging, as a single complete excision by an experienced surgeon, with counseling that ovarian surgery lowers the ovarian reserve and repeated operations should be avoided. [S]
Fertility: a preconception visit with folic acid before she stops the pill; try naturally once she is ready; refer to reproductive endocrinology if not pregnant after six months of trying. [S]
Pelvic floor physical therapy if deep pain with intercourse persists once the periods are suppressed. [S]
No opioids, benzodiazepines or sleep medicines; heat, regular exercise, and continued cognitive behavioral therapy for mood and sleep. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Whitlock, who sees her the same day. The ultrasound images were shown and explained to Ms. Monroe, who chose to continue medical treatment and was relieved that no operation is needed now; she decides who else receives this note. [S]
Follow-up: Gynecology review of the repeat ultrasound in about four months, or sooner if pain does not settle; Dr. Whitlock continues primary management. [S]
